name: application/http
description:
This type carries one or more complete HTTP request or response messages as a payload, registered in Section 10.2 of RFC 9112. The `msgtype` parameter says whether the enclosed messages are requests or responses, and `version` gives the HTTP version, though a reader can work both out from the first line.

It exists so HTTP messages can travel through something that is not an HTTP connection: batched into one request, stored, or attached to a report. [message/rfc822](/message/rfc822) does the equivalent job for a single email message.

name: application/scim+json
description:
SCIM, the System for Cross-domain Identity Management, is the protocol an identity provider uses to create, update and deactivate accounts in another service. RFC 7644 defines it, and this type marks its JSON payloads: users, groups, and the schema documents that describe what a resource may contain.

It is what sits behind automated user provisioning in enterprise single sign-on. The registration notes that older SCIM deployments send plain [application/json](/application/json) instead, so a server that wants to interoperate widely usually accepts both.

furtherReading.title: RFC 7644 - System for Cross-domain Identity Management: Protocol

name: application/linkset
description:
A linkset is a collection of web links published as its own document rather than crammed into an HTTP `Link` header. RFC 9264 defines it, and this form reuses the exact field syntax of that header, from RFC 8288, so the same text can be moved out of the response headers and served as a resource.

Header size is limited and links are sometimes numerous, which is the whole reason the format exists: a resource can point at its linkset instead of carrying every link on every response. The JSON serialisation is [application/linkset+json](/application/linkset+json).

furtherReading.title: RFC 9264 - Linkset: Media Types and a Link Relation Type for Link Sets

name: application/linkset+json
description:
The JSON serialisation of a linkset, a set of web links served as a document instead of squeezed into an HTTP `Link` header. RFC 9264 defines both forms. This one is an object whose sole member, `linkset`, holds an array of link context objects, each with an optional `anchor` and then one member per relation type listing the targets.

Most clients would rather parse this than the header field syntax used by [application/linkset](/application/linkset), which is the other form the same specification defines. The registration proposes no extension beyond the generic `.json`.

furtherReading.title: RFC 9264 - Linkset: Media Types and a Link Relation Type for Link Sets

name: application/reputon+json
description:
A reputon is one reputation score about one thing, defined by RFC 7071. The object names the subject being rated, the application the rating belongs to, the assertion being made about it, and a rating expressed as a floating-point value between 0.0 and 1.0 inclusive.

The application name is what gives the number meaning, and each one is registered separately: RFC 7072 defines the email identifier application, which rates a sending domain. Little else adopted the format, but it is the standard answer to a question that most services still answer with a bespoke JSON object.

furtherReading.title: RFC 7071 - A Media Type for Reputation Interchange

name: application/expect-ct-report+json
description:
The Expect-CT response header let a site ask browsers to enforce Certificate Transparency, and to report any certificate for it that had not been properly logged. This type marks those reports, which the browser posted to the address the header named. RFC 9163 documents the header and the report format as an Experimental specification.

The feature is finished. Only Chromium implemented it, and Chromium deprecated the header in version 107 on the grounds that it now enforces Certificate Transparency for every publicly trusted certificate anyway.
